title: God’s Glory in the Face of Christ; Treasure in Earthen Vessels
english: …our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

By this phrase our guide into the mysteries makes clear that faith is directed to God, even when it is exercised in the face of Christ. For both Jews and Greeks have been called to the knowledge of Christ: the one group, as it were, out of error and false worship into the true knowledge of God; the other, who were schooled under the Law, into a knowledge more exact than that of the Law. That is why the inspired Paul too is seen to have cared little for the lessons of the Law, “because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge” of Christ (Philippians 3:8).

Since, then, the guides into the mysteries preach Christ, and those who believe in God believe in the one God, and believe truly, how is Christ not God? He is not spurious, not falsely so called, not of another nature than the Father; rather, He is true God, as being from Him by nature.

The mind of those who go astray is filled with a darkness of the mind and with demonic deceit, but God promised that light would shine out of darkness for us (2 Corinthians 4:6). For He said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, “The people that sits in darkness, see a great light; you who dwell in the land and shadow of death, a light will shine on you” (Isaiah 9:2). And the inspired David says, as if speaking for those in gloom and darkness, “For You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, You will light up my darkness” (Psalm 18:28). Since the Father’s promise has now been fulfilled in us, and the divine light, seen by the mind, has dawned on us, we have come to know His glory in the face of Christ.

And then, if Christ is not God by nature and in truth, how have we beheld the Father’s glory in Him? Yet I plainly hear God the Father say, “My glory I will not give to another” (Isaiah 42:8); and see, He has given it to the Son. The Son, then, is not other than He, except in His own hypostasis and in His distinct existence; otherwise the Father would seem to have spoken falsely when He set His own glory in the face of the Son. It shows, too, that He who is God by nature is known both in Him and through Him. For the Son is the face and image and radiance of His hypostasis (Hebrews 1:3). The Son is revealed by the Father, and He in turn reveals the Father to us in Himself (Matthew 11:27).
Volume 3, Discourse 1.

“In earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). He calls the plainness of his speech “earthen vessels.” For the divine mysteries were not handed down to us in pompous words, but in the language that everyone is used to, so that all might learn and understand.

What then, Paul? Was it not within the power of God, who makes all wise, to make the holy apostles exceedingly eloquent with ease, far more polished in speech than those others, and skilled at stunning their hearers with the din of words? “Yes,” he says, “for He Himself is the giver of wisdom.” But He has shut up the divine treasure for us in earthen vessels, that is, in a lowly form. For what reason? “So that the surpassing greatness of the power may be of God and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

For in this way the apostles persuaded all to run to the faith. If their speech had been brilliant, it might at times have seemed that the faith of those who were called was not the work of His power. But since they persuaded with plain words, no one doubts that the surpassing power at work in this came from God.

By “earthen vessels” we mean the bodies we wear while we live among the things of sense, and we mean it in this way: since, while still clothed in flesh, which hinders the contemplation of the truth, we have the knowledge of the Trinity, the surpassing greatness of this knowledge is made known to us as coming not from ourselves but from the power of God.
“We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed,” and so on (2 Corinthians 4:8).

For they are seen to have endured even death itself for the sake of their devotion to Him. Yet even if this befell them, still they live, since they are to live to God. And, as the book of Wisdom says, “In the eyes of men they seemed…” (Wisdom of Solomon 3:2).

“In a lowly form”: the printed Greek ἐν ἕξει μικρῷ is probably corrupt, perhaps for ἐν λέξει μικρᾷ (“in humble speech”); the English covers either reading.

title: The Dying and the Life of Jesus
english: “…to have died, and their departure was counted an affliction, and their going from us a ruin; but they are at peace, and their hope is full of immortality” (Wisdom of Solomon 3:2–4). What, then, is the meaning of their toils? Paul explains it again, saying, “Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our body” (2 Corinthians 4:10).

We say that the dying meant here is to be understood in two ways: one is inward and spiritual, the other is taken as something felt in the body. For the Only-begotten Word of God, being God and having come forth from God by nature, made His own the flesh that is from the earth, and clothed Himself with this mortal human body, having also a rational soul. And what was the reason for this? That He might put sin to death in the flesh, and blunt the sting of the impulses inborn in it that carry us away to improper pleasures.

It was not for His own sake that the Word, being God, achieved this, that He should be seen above the passions that are in us; for He knows no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). Rather, He was, as it were, refashioning the whole of human nature in Himself into a holy and blameless life, when He became man and took the form that is ours. For He became “first in all things” (Colossians 1:18), so that we too, following in His steps (1 Peter 2:21), might have His dying in ourselves, that is, the power of sin made idle in the flesh, and so might be able to take up the blamelessness that leads to life.

You may also take the dying and the life of Jesus spoken of here in another way. For He became obedient to God the Father, as it is written, even to death itself (Philippians 2:8), and He laid down His life for the sheep (John 10:11). Yet “He died to sin once for all” (Romans 6:10), that is, for the sin of the world, for He has been set forth as a propitiation through faith (Romans 3:25); “but the life He lives, He lives to God” (Romans 6:10).

This dying, then, which passes through sufferings and reaches even to death itself, the guides into the mysteries carry about in their own bodies, “so that the life of Jesus,” as he himself says, “may be made manifest in our bodies” (2 Corinthians 4:10). For they too will live to God the holy, blameless, and blessed life.

That he is speaking here specifically of this dying, and of this life, is confirmed for the present by the sense of the preceding verses, which recount the trials and toils that anyone who wishes to complete the glorious course of the apostleship must endure. And he will persuade us no less to think so, all but explaining to his readers what he had said; for he at once adds what follows: “For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake,” and so on (2 Corinthians 4:11).

By these words he shows that they gladly choose to endure the death of the flesh for the sake of their devotion to Christ. For their aim is not to look at present things, but rather to look ahead to what is to come and to the rewards of their toils. They count as nothing the sweat of their struggles and rejoice instead in the good things from above, for they reckon how wide is God’s generosity. This is why they are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, “so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in the mortal flesh” (2 Corinthians 4:11).

And what is the life of Jesus? Incorruption and holiness, and a great glory beyond this world. For so it will be seen by us in its own time, when He comes down to us from above, from heaven, as Judge. And He will “transform the body of our lowliness, to be conformed to the body of His glory, by the working by which He is able even to subject all things to Himself” (Philippians 3:21).

“So death is at work in us, but life in you” (2 Corinthians 4:12). For the guides into the mysteries for the whole world under the sun have imitated their own Master: they too have laid down their lives, so that we who once went astray might gain the life that comes from faith in Christ. That is why…
translator_notes: Opens inside the quotation of Wisdom of Solomon 3:2–4 begun at the end of the previous section.
Cyril gives two readings of “the dying of Jesus” (2 Corinthians 4:10): the inward putting to death of sin, which Christ achieved for our nature, and the apostles' sharing in His sufferings and death.
“And so on” renders κ.τ.λ., by which Cyril cuts short the verse he is quoting.
The section ends on the word τοιγάρτοι (“That is why…”); the sentence continues in the next section.

title: Inner Renewal and the House from Heaven
english: …they say, in the voice of the psalmist, as though speaking to our Lord Jesus Christ, “For Your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psalm 44:22; Romans 8:36).
Volume 3, Discourse 2.
“Therefore we do not lose heart; but though our outer self is wasting away, yet the inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

One may approach the sense of these words aptly by setting the matter out as common, so to speak, to all who have chosen to live in godliness. For “the flesh wars against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other,” as it is written (Galatians 5:17). We say, then, that it is altogether necessary that when the flesh has in some way wasted away and its impulses have grown weak, then above all the other, that is, the mind of the Spirit (Romans 8:6), should grow all the stronger.

The word “Therefore” introduces the giving of a reason, a kind of reminder of something said before. He has said, then: If “we who live are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may be made manifest” in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:11), then, he says, since we hold this hope and rejoice in what is to come, we do not lose heart, for we see ahead of time the beauty of the glory to come; rather, even if affliction comes upon us, we bear it nobly. For even if, being human, we feel pain and suffer some harm in the body, still we are not overcome by these things, for our inner self is being renewed.
This, then, is the sense that applies to all. So when our outer self wastes away through the labors of spiritual discipline, then of necessity our inner self is renewed day by day.

But you may also take these words in another way. Because they proclaimed Jesus to Jews and Greeks alike, they endured terrible and unbearable persecutions, and their bodies were worn down by the labors this involved. But the greater the labor, the more abundant, I think, would be the repayment of grace that fittingly follows.

“For our momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

He strengthens the resolve of those who wish to compete, making little of the contests while exalting the crowns of the victors, and assigning lightness to the afflictions but weight to the glory. For the assault of the things of this life is measured, because it is temporary, even if it should come “beyond all measure”; yet he says that it will issue in an eternal weight of glory, since the good things of the age to come are beyond words. So we must not look at the things that are seen, which are temporary, but at the things that are unseen, which are eternal.

“For we know that if the earthly house of our tent is destroyed,” and so on (2 Corinthians 5:1). By “the earthly house of our tent” he names, in a roundabout way, the tent itself, that is, the body. For it is written in Job, “But those who dwell in houses of clay, of whom we too are, made of the same clay” (Job 4:19).

So, he says, we know that when death has destroyed the earthly house of our tent, that is, the body, the dwelling from heaven, that is, incorruption, will take its place before long, at the time of the resurrection, clearly. He says that it is from above, first because the gift is given by God; and then, besides, because all who dwell in the city above, I mean the ranks of the holy angels, are in incorruptible and imperishable bodies, for the nature of angels is free of this earthly grossness. So it is incorruption that he calls “a building from God,” “a house not made with hands,” and “eternal” as well (2 Corinthians 5:1).
“For in this we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:2). That is why we groan, weighed down as we are by corruption, and we long for what is from above…
